source.title: Do We Need Zero Training Loss After Achieving Zero Training Error?
source.authors: Takashi Ishida; Ikko Yamane; Tomoya Sakai; Gang Niu; Masashi Sugiyama

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether changing training after memorization affects test performance, using flooding rather than the claim versions' specified methods or measures.
record.gate_note: The paper tests flooding on synthetic and image datasets and reports test accuracy, training accuracy, loss curves, and gradient or flatness measurements. These findings do not test any listed version as specifically stated: there are no random-label experiments, width sweeps, convolution-versus-fully-connected comparisons, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout tests, magnitude-aware sharpness rankings against train-test gaps, or example-removal experiments.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates flooding, a new regularizer, rather than any listed claim version. Natural-label memorization does not establish random-label capacity (V1); epoch-wise test-loss descent does not test widening (V2); gradient amplitudes and qualitative loss slices do not measure magnitude-aware sharpness against generalization gaps (V7). The remaining versions' comparisons are absent. Listed findings provide background rather than a tool used by the method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate with a qualification: the authors report improvements across various datasets, rather than every configuration. They conclude that selected flood levels often preserve zero training error while avoiding near-zero training loss, and that flooding can induce epoch-wise double descent of test loss. Their explanation through flatter loss landscapes is tentative; they also prove reduced risk-estimator MSE under stated conditions.
record.recipe_differences: Flooding changes the objective to reverse gradients below a chosen positive loss level; the experiments use standard training on natural or synthetic labels, not the listed versions' interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The flooding benefit varies by dataset and setup: some benchmark configurations show slightly lower accuracy or a zero optimal flood level; results also vary with label noise and early stopping.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation-selected flooding often improves test accuracy, with benefits varying across datasets, noise levels, regularizers, and early stopping. Some configurations decline slightly or select zero flooding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Keeping training loss near a selected positive level can improve classification accuracy in some training regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.1 and Figure 3 report that validation-selected flood levels often preserve zero training error on natural-label benchmarks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Positive training loss can coexist with zero training error and improved held-out performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 2 and 6 show epoch-wise double descent of test loss under flooding in many settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Flooding can induce a second decline in test loss during continued training.

fits_no_version.finding: Sections 5.2–5.3 report changes in filter-normalized gradient amplitudes and qualitatively flatter loss slices during flooding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Flooding can change gradient amplitudes and local loss geometry alongside improved test performance.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: Table 3 reports no uncertainty estimates. Several reported flooding gains are small, and the paper does not provide numerical values in the text for the loss-curve and flatness figures. Synthetic data are also included, so findings do not all come from natural data.
record.rows_left_out: No omitted applicable table rows. Figure-based learning curves and gradient/flatness plots were not extracted as separate rows because the versions do not measure those specific quantities, and the relevant values are figure-only.

untested.parts: No fixed random-label fit or random-label held-out control; fitting natural labels with zero error does not test the claimed coexistence.
No width sweep beyond interpolation. The reported double descent varies epochs and measures test loss.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison on the same image task or local-connectivity intervention.
No controlled adaptive-optimizer-versus-SGD comparison or tuning comparison.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted recipes.
No dropout intervention, dropout-rate sweep, or joint dropout/weight-decay removal.

No magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance versus training-error threshold, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures. Gradient amplitudes and one-dimensional loss slices measure different quantities.
No influence-based memorization estimates, example removal, or retraining against random-removal controls.

record.verdict_notes: All table accuracy values and baselines match the supplied text. States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because these rows measure flooding performance rather than a listed effect; they do not indicate that the table values are unreadable. The figure findings are already declared in rows_left_out and do not require missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
No width sweep around the zero-training-error threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.

The paper measures filter-normalized gradient amplitude and visualizes loss under perturbation, but does not test whether magnitude-aware sharpness ranks train-test gaps against the specified alternative measures.
